The quark constituents became matter fields in the theory of strong interactions.
The successful quantum electromagnetic theory became part of the broader electroweak description.
Particle fields and their interactions supply the model’s common formal framework.
Critical behavior in many-particle systems motivated Wilson’s scaling analysis.
Field-theory renormalization supplied methods later connected with critical phenomena.
Difficulties applying familiar field-theory methods to hadron scattering motivated alternative dual models.
String descriptions retain quantum principles while changing the objects being quantized.
Joint quantum states permit correlations that cannot be reduced to independent states for the parts.
Experimental tests compare correlations and joint outcome probabilities.
Greco-Egyptian alchemy combined theories of material transformation with craft practices.
Metalworking supplied practical transformations and apparatus for alchemical investigation.
Earlier material-transformation traditions formed part of the setting for phlogiston accounts of metals and burning.
Oxygen chemistry replaced the release of phlogiston with combination with a component of air.
Quantitative weighing and gas collection distinguished oxygen uptake from hypothetical material loss.
Accounting for gases helped make mass balance explicit in the chemical revolution.
Closed-vessel weighing reveals whether all reactants and products have been counted.
Quantitative mass relationships constrain possible combinations of atoms.
Dalton’s work on gases and relative masses helped shape his atomic program.
Both accounts use discrete constituents, but Dalton’s theory introduced quantitative chemical tests; this edge compares frameworks rather than asserting direct transmission.
Pressure and volume instruments make numerical relationships in air experimentally accessible.
Proportionalities among gas variables can be combined and rearranged as equations.
Distinguishing molecules from atoms resolved conflicts in combining-gas ratios.
Measured gas-volume ratios motivated a molecular interpretation of equal volumes.
Electrical currents provide a controllable way to drive chemical transformations.
Electrolysis isolated additional elements and helped reveal families with similar properties.
Elemental composition and atomic groupings made organic reactions amenable to chemical analysis.
Isomers and persistent atomic groupings highlighted the importance of molecular arrangement.
Structural formulas specify arrangements of the atoms already used to represent composition.
Relative atomic masses supplied an early quantitative axis for ordering the elements.
Cannizzaro’s use of molecular ideas clarified atomic masses before major periodic classifications.
Reacting particles and their concentrations supply a microscopic interpretation of reaction rates.
Rate laws become equations for how concentrations change with time.
Quantitative composition measurements reveal stable ratios in reversible reactions.
Equal forward and reverse rates explain how constant composition can coexist with continuing molecular reactions.
Gibbs extended thermodynamic reasoning to reacting mixtures and coexisting phases.
Entropy and energy together determine equilibrium criteria under suitable constraints.
Chemical potentials generalize equilibrium relationships beyond simple concentration-based rules.
Tetrahedral geometry added spatial distinctions to earlier connectivity formulas.
Three-dimensional arrangements and mirror symmetry distinguish molecular configurations.
The electron supplied the constituent that Lewis used to explain valence and shared pairs.
Electron pairs supplied a proposed physical explanation for the bonds in structural formulas.
Recurring outer-shell patterns help explain recurring valences across element groups.
Lewis’s acid–base definition uses electron-pair donation and acceptance.
Reversible proton transfer can be quantified with equilibrium constants.
The molecular Schrödinger problem turns quantum principles into predictions about chemical bonds.
Quantum states provide an explanation for electron-pair bonding beyond the original Lewis picture.
Molecular orbitals are one quantum framework for describing electrons distributed across atoms.
Linear combinations of atomic states provide approximate molecular orbitals.
Long covalent chains extend structural chemistry from small molecules to macromolecules.
Covalent connectivity distinguishes a macromolecule from a loose aggregate of small molecules.
Controlled separation and comparison of fractions turn mixtures into experimentally distinguishable components.
The laboratory study of organic substances supplied methods and questions for cell-free biochemical reactions.
Enzymes explain how fermentation can proceed through catalysts in extracts without intact living cells.
Comparing otherwise similar reactions reveals acceleration by a substance that is regenerated.
